title: Sunken Ark Hall
subject: Contracts
subtopic: Assumption of risk for unknown subsurface conditions
stem:
Lydia owned a private, for-profit Christian family camp called Mustard Seed Adventures. For an agreed price of $8 million, Barnabas Construction, a company specializing in large themed projects and excavation, contracted to design and build on Lydia’s lakeside parcel a Noah’s-Ark-shaped indoor climbing hall. Because sinkholes were common in the area, a local safety ordinance required the hall’s foundation and underground utilities to be excavated at least 18 feet.

Barnabas began digging and, at 11 feet, encountered a continuous shelf of limestone. When the contract was made, neither Lydia nor Barnabas knew of the limestone, and neither had hired a geotechnical expert to test for subsurface rock. Barnabas accurately claimed that removing enough limestone to build as planned would cost an additional $1.2 million and would probably leave it with a net loss of $800,000 on the job. Barnabas refused to continue unless Lydia promised to pay an additional $1 million for the completed hall.

If Lydia refuses and sues Barnabas for breach of contract, which of the following will the court probably decide?
call: If Lydia refuses and sues Barnabas for breach of contract, which of the following will the court probably decide?

choices.A: Barnabas is excused, because the contract is voidable on account of the parties’ mutual mistake concerning an essential underlying fact.
choices.B: Lydia prevails, because Barnabas assumed the risk of encountering subsurface limestone that was unknown to Lydia.
choices.C: Lydia prevails, because Barnabas did not know that subsurface limestone was present in the area.
choices.D: Barnabas is excused under the modern doctrine of supervening impossibility, which includes severe impracticability.

rightExplanation: B is correct. Lydia should prevail because Barnabas was the specialist, accepted a fixed price, knew deep excavation was required, and skipped available subsurface testing. Gold Key: risk beats surprise. A contractor who takes a fixed-price excavation job while treating limited site knowledge as enough usually carries the unknown-site-condition risk. Silver Key: read the answer array as outcome plus reason. Do not stop at “owner wins”; the because-clause must put the risk bucket on the right party.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: This is anchor-assisted. The choice gives the attractive mutual-mistake label but omits the risk condition. A student cannot kill it as hard structure alone; the Gold Key supplies the missing tiny anchor.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: This is student-accessible Issue-Sense. The fact is true, but it is not responsive. “Barnabas did not know” does not explain why Lydia wins. The answer fails the because-clause test.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: This is anchor-assisted. The choice stretches impracticability too far. The stem gives a cost increase and probable loss, but the Gold Key keeps fixed-price construction risk in the contractor’s bucket.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: B remains. It is true and responsive: it names the party who carried the subsurface-risk bucket.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Not needed after the anchor-assisted Cut.

studentScript: Fixed price. Specialist excavator. Deep digging required. No testing. Surprise rock and more cost do not automatically excuse. Pick the answer that names risk assumed: B.

A.signal: Both parties' ignorance is attractive, but the answer omits who carried the risk.
A.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 152 and 154 make risk allocation fatal to mutual mistake avoidance.

B.signal: The because-clause names the risk bucket.
B.lawyer: The contractor's specialization, required excavation, opportunity to test, and fixed-price undertaking support allocating the unknown-site-condition risk to the contractor.

C.signal: No actual knowledge is not the reason Lydia wins.
C.lawyer: Actual ignorance does not prevent risk allocation to the contractor under the mistake-risk rule.

D.signal: The added cost is real, but the answer over-extends the excuse.
D.lawyer: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 261 does not treat ordinary fixed-price construction cost increases as enough for impracticability.

goldKeys.statement: Risk beats surprise: a specialist who takes a fixed-price excavation job, knows digging is required, and skips available testing usually carries the unknown-site-condition risk.
goldKeys.trigger: Specialized contractor + fixed price + required excavation + no subsurface test + moderate added cost.
goldKeys.unlocks: The mutual-mistake and impracticability traps by separating unknown facts from assumed risk.

silverKeys.statement: Read the array as outcome plus reason. Do not stop at 'excused' or 'owner prevails'; keep the answer whose because-clause puts the subsurface-risk bucket on the right party.
silverKeys.trigger: Two answers excuse the contractor and two answers favor the owner.
silverKeys.unlocks: The 2x2 outcome/reason array: excuse theories versus owner-prevails reasons.

remediation.title: Risk bucket beats surprise
remediation.signal: Specialist contractor, fixed price, required excavation, no testing, and moderate cost increase.
remediation.studentMove: Ask who carried the risk before asking whether the surprise was mutual or expensive.
remediation.tinyRule: Unknown subsurface conditions usually stay with the specialist contractor when the contractor had the chance to test and priced the job anyway.
remediation.trap: Mutual-mistake and impracticability answers that omit assumption of risk.
